name: Serbian nationalism
summary: Serbian nationalism is an ethnic nationalism holding that Serbs form one nation whose cultural and political unity should be secured, ideally in a single state. It centres on the Kosovo myth, the Serbian Orthodox Church as the core of national identity, opposition to the secession of territories claimed as Serbian, and a Greater Serbia tradition running from Garasanin's 1844 programme through the 1986 Memorandum to the Radical Party and Dveri. Today's parties are Eurosceptic, anti-NATO, Russia-leaning and socially conservative.

apologise-for-past-wrongs.rationale: The Memorandum demands that the "burden of historical guilt" be removed from the Serbian nation and rejects the "symmetry in historical guilt" and the imposed guilt complex.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Korkmaz describes the "Greater Serbia" ideal as not bound to legally defined territory and grounded in historical, democratic and demographic legitimacy, and Pešić describes a national programme to unite all Serbs in one state, pursued through wars and annexation of "Serbian lands".

decide-locally.rationale: Gligorov says nationalist economics in Serbia tended towards centralism rather than territorial and fiscal decentralization.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Korkmaz says Serbian nationalists, foreseeing difficulty keeping peace in a Greater Serbia where Serbs would not be a majority, came up with a "homogeneous Serbia".

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Tot says the "First Serbia" bloc, represented intellectually by Academy members such as Ćosić and Bećković, believes Serbia should be militarily neutral, with a preference for a strategic and cultural alliance with Russia.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Memorandum states that "no form of political oppression and discrimination on the basis of nationality is properly acceptable in modern society" and laments that nations and nationalities are not equal before the law.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Korkmaz says Serbian nationalists developed the idea of a "homogeneous Serbia" and later an ethnically pure country, and Vujadinović says the Memorandum's line implied ethnic homogenization and an ethnic state of all Serbs.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Pešić says the Serbian national position defended Serbian territory against minorities by force and kept authoritarian structures as necessary until the national question was solved, opening an internal front in Kosovo.

free-trade.rationale: Gligorov describes Serbian economic nationalism as reduced to protectionism, the opposite of a free-trade policy.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Korkmaz and Pešić describe Kosovo as Serbia's "historical right" as the medieval centre of the Serbs, even though few Serbs now live there, and Saggau describes the Kosovo covenant myth as a Serbian entitlement to the land.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Saggau shows Serbian Orthodox texts calling Kosovo the Serbian "Jerusalem" and "Holy Land" under a covenant entitling a people to holy soil, and Ramet and Günal report two-thirds of Serbs treating Kosovo as the "heart of Serbia".

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Saggau shows the Kosovo narrative centres on Prince Lazar's martyrdom, with the church's cult of Lazar presenting the Serbs as a "martyr-nation".

minority-language-support.rationale: The Memorandum protests that Serbs living in other republics lack the right to use their own language and alphabet and to organize culturally, and treats the loss of Cyrillic as a grievance.

more-religion-public.rationale: Tot describes a "deep synthesis of the national and the religious" with deep reverence for the Serbian Orthodox Church, and Duijzings shows religion fused with national identity at the centre of nationalist discourse.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The Memorandum praises the principle of "political and cultural autonomy of nationalities and national minorities" and complains that Serbs outside Serbia cannot organize politically and culturally.

national-rebirth.rationale: The Memorandum says the Serbian nation must "find itself again" and become a historical agent after its defeats, and Miller shows that the call for a Serbian renaissance was the one point nearly the whole intelligentsia agreed on in the late 1980s.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Memorandum protests that the Serbian nation alone was left "without its own state like all of the other nations" and calls its lack of one the greatest calamity, while also asking that every nation in Yugoslavia be allowed to state its intentions.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Pešić says Serbia defended Kosovo "as its historical right" and Ramet and Günal show Serbia insisting that Kosovo is rightfully part of Serbia ("Kosovo is Serbia"), although Vučić showed limited flexibility in 2013.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Tot describes the nationalist and traditionalist "First Serbia" bloc as Euroskeptic and shows its press casting the EU as a threat to Serbian identity.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The 1986 SANU Memorandum calls the integrity of the Serbian nation and its culture "vital to its survival and progress" and protests that Serbian cultural achievements are being usurped, displaced and denigrated; Miller reads its call for national revival as the common aim of the Serbian intelligentsia.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: The Memorandum treats the position of Serbs living outside Serbia, especially in Croatia, as an urgent political question and complains the homeland cannot even keep informed of them; Dimitrijević records that the Serbian state claimed to represent the interests of all Serbs wherever they lived.

public-ownership.rationale: Gligorov says that at the end of the 1980s Serbian nationalist politics advocated a greater state role in the economy and supported nationalization over privatization.

religious-nation.rationale: Duijzings says that since the early nineteenth century Orthodox religion and Serb identity have fused and Orthodoxy became central to Serbianness, although Karadžić argued for a language-based definition; Tot calls this synthesis religious nationalism.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: In the Kosovo myth Lazar accepts death and defeat rather than submit, and Ramet and Günal say the myth imposes an implicit oath on Serbs to keep fighting for Kosovo.

sacred-nation.rationale: Tot, citing Bakić, says "St Sava nationalism" posits the nation as "holy", and Saggau describes the Serbs and their nation as portrayed as holy warriors in the Kosovo myth.

separate-church-state.rationale: Patalakh describes the Serbian national idea as an organic unity or "symphony" of state, church and people, and Tot describes a deep synthesis of the national and the religious.

single-official-language.rationale: The Memorandum objects that an official language bearing another nation's name was made obligatory for Serbs in Croatia and says Serbs elsewhere must be able to use their own language and alphabet.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Tot says the "First Serbia" bloc, represented intellectually by Academy members such as Ćosić and Bećković, holds that Serbia should be a militarily neutral country.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Gligorov calls protectionism "the favorite trade policy of nationalists" and says Serbian economic nationalism is reduced to protectionism.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Korkmaz says the nineteenth-century idea that a strong state needs wide territory drove Garašanin's national programme for Greater Serbia, and Pešić says Serbia was inspired by expanding to reclaim historical territories.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Saggau describes the Kosovo narratives as an antiquity myth linking the medieval Serbian state to the present, and Ramet and Günal note the reading that the Kosovo choice entitles Serbs to restore rule over all lands lost in medieval times.

scope: The mainstream Serbian ethnic-national tradition that the defining sources call Serbian nationalism: Vuk Karadžić's language-based definition of the Serbs, Garašanin's Načertanije programme of 1844 as its first national programme, the Kosovo myth, the 1986 SANU Memorandum as compiling its central theses (s8, s9), and its post-1990 political forms (s10, s11, s14, s17). The sources document national, territorial, religious and foreign-policy positions far better than economic or social ones, so the answers cover those and leave the rest null. It leaves out the platforms of individual parties and organisations as such (a party's programme holds more than the ideology), the Yugoslavist reading of Garašanin and Karadžić, and Serbian liberal or socialist thought that rejects the ethnic national frame.
